stem: What does `typeof null` return in JavaScript?

options.text: "object"
"null"
"undefined"
"number"

explanation: `typeof null` returns "object". This is a long-standing quirk of the language, so check for null with `=== null`.

stem: Which array method returns a NEW array containing only the elements that pass a test?

options.text: forEach
filter
push
reduce

explanation: `filter` builds a new array of the elements for which the callback returns true. `forEach` returns undefined and `push` mutates.

stem: In a loop `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }`, what is printed?

options.text: Nothing is printed

explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so all callbacks share one `i`. The callbacks run after the loop ends, when `i` is 3. Using `let` gives 0, 1, 2.

stem: What does an `async` function always return?

options.text: The value it returns, directly
undefined
A callback
A Promise

explanation: An async function always wraps its result in a Promise, even if you return a plain value.

stem: What is the output order? `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`

options.text: A, D, C, B
A, B, C, D
A, D, B, C
A, C, D, B

explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before timer callbacks (macrotasks), so C comes before B.

stem: What does `[1, 2, 3].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n)` evaluate to when no initial value is given?

options.text: A TypeError is thrown

explanation: Without an initial value, `acc` starts as the first element (1) and iteration begins at the second element: 1+2+3 = 6.

stem: Which element is the most appropriate for the main navigation links of a page?

options.text: <div>
<section>
<nav>
<aside>

explanation: `<nav>` marks a block of navigation links and is exposed to assistive technology as a navigation landmark.

stem: Which CSS declaration makes an element a flex container?

options.text: flex: container;
position: flex;
float: flex;
display: flex;

explanation: `display: flex` turns the element into a flex container so its children become flex items.

stem: Which meta tag is needed so a page lays out correctly on a phone?

options.text: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<meta name="mobile-friendly" content="true; width=device">
<meta charset="mobile" content="device-width, scale=1">
<meta name="responsive" content="on, width=device-width">

explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to use the device width instead of a zoomed-out desktop width.

stem: In a flex row container, which property aligns items along the MAIN axis (horizontally)?

options.text: align-items
justify-content
align-content
flex-wrap

explanation: `justify-content` distributes items along the main axis. `align-items` works on the cross axis.

stem: Why prefer `<button>` over `<div onclick=...>` for an action?

options.text: It downloads and renders noticeably faster than a div does
It ignores every CSS rule that the author applies to it
It is focusable, keyboard-operable and announced as a button by default
It is the only element that can receive a click event in the DOM

explanation: A native button gives keyboard support (Enter/Space), focus handling and the correct accessibility role for free.

stem: What does `@media (min-width: 768px) { ... }` do?

options.text: Applies the rules only when the viewport is narrower than 768px
Forces the page container to be exactly 768px wide at all times
Hides the whole page whenever the viewport is under 768px
Applies the rules only when the viewport is at least 768px wide

explanation: `min-width` queries match when the viewport is at least that wide, which is the basis of a mobile-first approach.

stem: Node.js executes your JavaScript code on:

options.text: A single main thread driven by an event loop
One new thread for every incoming request
A thread pool that runs all of your own code
Multiple worker processes started by default

explanation: Node runs JavaScript on one thread and uses the event loop plus libuv's thread pool for I/O work.

stem: Which file lists a project's dependencies and scripts?

options.text: node_modules
package.json
index.html
npm.config

explanation: `package.json` records metadata, scripts and dependencies. `node_modules` holds the installed packages.

stem: What is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?

options.text: dependencies are installed only on production servers, never locally
They behave identically; the split is only a naming convention
devDependencies are only needed for development and build, such as test tools
devDependencies are installed globally rather than inside node_modules

explanation: Packages needed to run the app go in `dependencies`. Tools used only to develop or test go in `devDependencies`.

stem: Why use `fs.createReadStream` for a very large file instead of `fs.readFileSync`?

options.text: It is always faster than readFileSync, even for tiny files
It blocks the event loop until the whole file is loaded
It compresses the file on disk before reading it
It processes the file in chunks without loading it all into memory

explanation: Streams read data in chunks, which keeps memory use low. `readFileSync` loads everything and blocks the event loop.

stem: What happens if you run a long CPU-heavy loop in an Express request handler?

options.text: The event loop is blocked and other requests wait
Node starts a new thread automatically
Only that request is slow
Express rejects the request

explanation: Synchronous CPU work monopolises the single thread, so every other request is stalled. Use worker threads or offload the work.

stem: Which runs first in Node: `process.nextTick` callbacks or Promise `.then` callbacks?

options.text: Promise callbacks
process.nextTick callbacks
setTimeout callbacks
They run at the same time

explanation: The nextTick queue is drained before the promise microtask queue, and both run before timers.

stem: Which command stages all changes in the current directory for the next commit?

options.text: git add .
git commit .
git push .
git stage --all

explanation: 'git add .' stages every changed file under the current directory. commit and push operate on already-staged/committed changes; 'git stage --all' is not a standard git command.

stem: Which command creates a new branch named 'feature-x' and switches to it in one step?

options.text: git checkout -b feature-x
git branch feature-x
git merge feature-x
git switch feature-x

explanation: 'checkout -b' creates the branch and switches to it immediately. 'git branch' alone only creates it without switching; 'git switch feature-x' without -c would fail since the branch doesn't exist yet.

stem: You ran `git commit -m 'fix bug'` but forgot to stage a changed file. After staging that file with `git add`, which command adds it into the previous commit instead of creating a new one?

options.text: git commit --amend
git commit --fixup
git rebase -i
git cherry-pick

explanation: 'git commit --amend' replaces the most recent commit with a new one that includes the currently staged changes. The other commands either prepare a separate fixup commit or operate on commit history/ranges, not the immediately preceding commit.

stem: Which command downloads commits from a remote repository WITHOUT merging them into your current branch?

options.text: git fetch
git pull
git clone
git push

explanation: git fetch updates your local copy of the remote's branches without touching your working branch. git pull is fetch followed by merge; clone is for an initial copy, not ongoing sync; push sends commits, it doesn't download them.

stem: During a merge, git reports a conflict in file.txt. After manually editing the file to resolve the conflict, what are the next two steps?

options.text: git add file.txt, then git commit
git checkout file.txt, then git push
git reset file.txt, then git merge --continue
git stash, then git merge --abort

explanation: After hand-resolving a conflict, staging the file with 'git add' marks it resolved, and 'git commit' completes the merge. 'git checkout file.txt' would discard your edits; 'reset' unstages rather than resolves; 'merge --abort' cancels the merge entirely.

stem: What does `git push --force` risk that `git push --force-with-lease` protects against?

options.text: Overwriting remote commits that someone else pushed since your last fetch
Losing your own local uncommitted changes in the working tree
Deleting the remote branch entirely along with its history
Corrupting the local .git directory and its object store

explanation: '--force-with-lease' checks that the remote branch still points where you last saw it before overwriting, so it refuses the push if someone else has pushed in the meantime. Plain '--force' overwrites blindly, which can silently discard a teammate's commits.

stem: When does TypeScript check types?

options.text: At run time, while the code is executing
Only when the formatting rules are checked
At compile time, before the code runs
While network requests are being sent

explanation: TypeScript's checks happen during compilation. The emitted JavaScript contains no type information.

stem: Which declaration defines an object type with a name and an age?

options.text: const Person = { name: string, age: number }
type Person = name: string, age: number
class Person => { name: string; age: number; id: string }
interface Person { name: string; age: number }

explanation: An interface (or type alias) describes the shape of an object. The other forms are not valid TypeScript.

stem: What is the type of x inside the if block? function f(x: string | number) { if (typeof x === 'string') { x; } }

options.text: string
number
string | number
never

explanation: A typeof check narrows a union. Inside the block the compiler knows x is a string.

stem: What does function first<T>(items: T[]): T mean?

options.text: It returns the first element converted into a string
It returns an element of the same type as the array's elements
It accepts only arrays that contain numbers
It returns a new array that holds just the first element of the input

explanation: T is a placeholder. Passing a string[] makes T a string, so the return type is string.

stem: Which is a safe way to handle a value of type unknown?

options.text: Assert it to any and call its methods directly
Cast it to the expected type without checking it
Narrow it with checks such as typeof before using it
Declare it as never so the compiler stops complaining

explanation: unknown forces you to prove what a value is before use. any and unchecked casts switch the safety off.

stem: What does T extends { id: number } do in a generic?

options.text: Makes T inherit all the run-time methods of an object literal
Requires T to be exactly the type { id: number }
Adds an id property to every value of type T
Restricts T to types that have a numeric id property

explanation: The constraint allows any type with at least an id: number, so the function can safely read item.id.

stem: Which call defines an Express route that handles GET requests to /users?

options.text: app.fetch('/users', handler)
app.route.get = '/users'
app.get('/users', handler)
app.users.get(handler)

explanation: Express exposes one method per HTTP verb, such as app.get and app.post, taking a path and a handler.

stem: Why validate request bodies on the server even if the front end already validates them?

options.text: Front-end checks are not allowed to run in browsers
Servers validate data faster than any browser can
HTTP forbids sending invalid data to a server
Clients can be bypassed, so the server must not trust its input

explanation: Anyone can send a request with curl and skip your form. The server is the only check you control.

stem: What happens if a middleware neither sends a response nor calls next()?

options.text: The request hangs until the client times out
Express sends a 404 automatically after a short delay
Express skips the middleware and moves on to the route
The server process exits with an error message

explanation: Express waits for either a response or next(). Doing neither leaves the request open.

stem: How does Express recognise an error-handling middleware?

options.text: It must always be registered before every other middleware
It is declared with four parameters: err, req, res and next
Its function name has to end with the word Handler
It is attached with app.catch instead of app.use

explanation: The four-argument signature is what marks it as an error handler, and it is registered after the routes.

stem: An async route handler in Express 4 throws inside an awaited call. What is needed so the error reaches the error middleware?

options.text: Nothing, because Express 4 forwards all async errors automatically
Return the error object as the response body directly
Catch it and pass it to next(err), or use a wrapper that does so
Call res.end() inside a finally block to close the response

explanation: Express 4 does not catch rejected promises. Without next(err) the request hangs or the process crashes.

stem: Which response is most appropriate when a JSON body fails validation?

options.text: 200 OK with an empty body to avoid leaking details
500 Internal Server Error with the full stack trace attached for debugging
404 Not Found because the expected data was missing
400 Bad Request with a message naming the invalid fields

explanation: 400 tells the client its request was wrong, and field-level messages let it fix the problem. A 500 would blame the server.

stem: In MongoDB, what is a document?

options.text: A row in a table with a fixed set of columns
A file stored in a directory on the server
A JSON-like record stored in a collection
A saved query together with its result set

explanation: Documents are BSON records with flexible fields, grouped into collections.

stem: What is the main purpose of an index in MongoDB?

options.text: To encrypt the fields stored in a collection
To limit how many documents a query can return
To back up the collection automatically
To speed up queries on the indexed fields

explanation: An index lets MongoDB find matching documents without scanning the whole collection, at some cost to writes.

stem: A blog post has a handful of comments that are always shown with it. Which model fits best?

options.text: Embed the comments as an array inside the post document
Store each comment in a separate database server
Keep comments in a separate collection with no link back to the post
Store only the comment count and discard the text

explanation: Data read together and bounded in size is usually embedded, which needs one read instead of many.

stem: Which pipeline computes the total sales per customer?

options.text: $match on customer followed by $skip
$group by customer with a $sum of the amount
$project the amount and then $limit to one
$sort by customer and then $unwind the amount

explanation: $group collects documents by a key and accumulators such as $sum compute totals for each group.

stem: A query filters on status and sorts by createdAt. Which compound index serves it best?

options.text: { createdAt: 1 } on its own
{ status: 1 } on its own
{ status: 1, createdAt: 1 }
{ createdAt: 1, status: 1 }

explanation: Equality fields come first, then the sort field, so MongoDB can jump to one status and read it already sorted.

stem: Why can unbounded arrays inside a document be a problem?

options.text: MongoDB cannot store arrays inside documents at all
Arrays are always sorted, which wastes processing time
Indexes cannot be created on a collection that has arrays
Documents have a 16 MB size limit and large arrays make updates slow

explanation: An array that keeps growing can hit the size limit. Reference child documents in their own collection instead.

stem: How should passwords be stored?

options.text: In plain text so support staff can recover them
As salted hashes made with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt
Encrypted with one single key that is stored right beside the data
As a fast unsalted MD5 hash of each password

explanation: Hashes cannot be reversed, salts defeat precomputed tables and a deliberately slow algorithm hampers guessing.

stem: A JSON Web Token has three parts. What are they?

options.text: Username, password and salt
Request line, response body and cookie jar
Header, payload and signature
Key, value and expiry

explanation: The header names the algorithm, the payload holds the claims and the signature proves it was not altered.

stem: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication decides what you may do; authorization proves who you are
They are two names for the same login check
Authentication happens on the client and authorization in the browser cache
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do

explanation: First the system identifies you, then it checks your role or permissions for each action.

stem: Why should passwords or other secrets not be put in a JWT payload?

options.text: The payload is only encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it
The payload is encrypted but too small to hold much data
Tokens are deleted by the server after a single request
JWT libraries refuse to sign any payloads that contain plain strings

explanation: Base64 encoding is not encryption. A signed token is tamper-proof, not secret.

stem: Why add a unique salt to each password before hashing?

options.text: The hash can then be reversed when a user forgets the password
Identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables stop working
Hashing runs faster on large tables of users
The password becomes encrypted instead of hashed

explanation: Without salts, two users with the same password share a hash and one rainbow table cracks every account.

stem: A JWT access token is valid for 7 days and a user's account is then disabled. What is the risk?

options.text: None, because disabling an account invalidates every issued token
The token stops working as soon as the user logs in elsewhere
The token still works until it expires unless the server also checks a deny list
The token becomes valid for read operations only

explanation: Stateless tokens are not looked up on each request. Use short lifetimes with refresh tokens, or a revocation check.

stem: What does an Angular component combine?

options.text: A database schema, a route definition and a unit test
A server, a client and a compiler
A TypeScript class, a template and styles
A service, a pipe and a build script

explanation: The class holds the logic, the template the markup and the styles the look of one piece of the interface.

stem: Which syntax is property binding in an Angular template?

options.text: (value)="name"
{{value}}="name"
#value="name"
[value]="name"

explanation: Square brackets bind a component value to an element property. Parentheses bind events.

stem: How does Angular give a component access to a service?

options.text: It injects the service instance through the component's constructor
The component creates it with new inside its template
The service is copied into each template at compile time
Components import a global variable that is named after the service

explanation: Angular's injector creates and supplies instances, which keeps components loosely coupled and easy to test.

stem: What does [(ngModel)] do?

options.text: It binds from the template to the class only
It gives two-way binding between a form control and a component property
It runs an event handler only when the form is submitted
It adds or removes elements from the page structure

explanation: [(ngModel)] combines property binding and event binding, so changes flow in both directions.

stem: With OnPush change detection, when is a component checked again?

options.text: Whenever any timer fires anywhere in the application
Whenever the route changes, whatever its inputs are
When an input reference changes, an event fires in it, or it is marked for check
Whenever the browser window is resized by the user

explanation: OnPush skips a component unless its inputs change by reference or an event originates inside it, which saves work.

stem: What does providedIn: 'root' do for a service?

options.text: Creates a new instance for every component that injects it
Restricts the service to the root component only
Loads the service lazily when its own route opens
Registers one application-wide instance that can be tree-shaken if unused

explanation: A root-provided service is a singleton. The build can drop it if nothing injects it.

stem: When does an Observable start producing values?

options.text: As soon as the file that defines it is loaded
When the component's template finishes rendering
When something subscribes to it
Only after the first operator is added to it

explanation: Observables are lazy. Nothing happens until subscribe() is called.

stem: What is a Subject in RxJS?

options.text: A function that converts a promise into a plain number value
An operator that delays values by one second
A component that displays streamed data
An observable that can also be pushed values with next()

explanation: A Subject is both an observable and an observer, so you can multicast values to many subscribers.

stem: Which operator transforms each emitted value into a new value?

options.text: map
filter
take
tap

explanation: map applies a function to every value. filter drops values, take limits how many pass and tap only performs side effects.

stem: How does a BehaviorSubject differ from a plain Subject?

options.text: It only emits the very first value that was pushed
It holds a current value and gives it to new subscribers immediately
It completes after the first subscriber disconnects
It cannot be subscribed to more than once

explanation: Late subscribers to a BehaviorSubject get the latest value straight away, which suits state.

stem: In a type-ahead search, which operator cancels the previous request when a new value arrives?

options.text: mergeMap
concatMap
switchMap
exhaustMap

explanation: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner observable, so stale responses never overwrite newer ones.

stem: Why avoid mutating state objects in a store pattern?

options.text: JavaScript blocks mutation of objects inside modules
Immutable objects always use less memory than mutable ones
Stores can only hold primitive values such as numbers
Immutable updates make changes detectable and predictable for subscribers

explanation: Replacing the object lets reference checks and OnPush spot changes, and keeps past states for debugging.

stem: What does a unit test usually check?

options.text: The whole system running in production
One small piece of code in isolation
How fast the network connection is
Whether the interface looks pleasant

explanation: Unit tests are small and fast because they test one function or class with its dependencies controlled.

stem: Why mock an external API in a unit test?

options.text: So the test always passes whatever the code does
Because real APIs refuse requests from test runners
So the test is fast, repeatable and independent of the network
So the API provider can read the test results

explanation: A mock gives a controlled response, so failures point to your code and not to a slow or unavailable service.

stem: A project has 100% line coverage. What can you conclude?

options.text: The code contains no bugs of any kind
Every possible input has been tested
All branches and error paths are verified
Every line ran during the tests, but not that the assertions are meaningful

explanation: Coverage shows what executed, not what was checked. A test with no assertions still raises coverage.

stem: Which test best catches a mismatch between an API and its database schema?

options.text: An integration test that calls the API against a test database
A unit test with every dependency replaced by a mock
A linter rule that checks indentation in the files
A screenshot comparison of the home page

explanation: Only a test that uses the real database can notice that a column or type does not match.

stem: A test mocks the database and always passes, yet the real query is wrong. What is the lesson?

options.text: Mocks should never be used in any kind of test
Mocks only verify your assumptions, so add an integration test for the real query
The test needs more mocks to cover more lines
Database queries cannot be tested automatically

explanation: A mock returns whatever you told it to, so it cannot show that the real query works.

stem: How are flaky tests best handled?

options.text: Re-run until they pass and ignore the failures
Delete the test so that the whole pipeline turns green again quickly
Find the cause, such as shared state or timing, and fix it
Add sleeps of several seconds to every test

explanation: Flaky tests hide real failures and teach people to ignore red builds. Fixing the cause restores trust.

stem: What is the purpose of a lint stage in CI?

options.text: To deploy the code to a staging server
To catch style problems and simple errors before tests run
To compress the images in the build output
To rotate the production database credentials

explanation: Linting is fast and gives early feedback on code quality before slower stages begin.

stem: A pipeline runs every night at 2 am. What kind of trigger is this?

options.text: A manual approval gate
A webhook from a pull request
A scheduled trigger
A dependency update event

explanation: Schedules start a pipeline at fixed times, which suits long tests or dependency checks.

stem: Why run fast unit tests before slow end-to-end tests?

options.text: End-to-end tests cannot run before unit tests exist
Unit tests are required by the CI provider's terms
Slow tests are only allowed to run after the deployment has finished
Cheap failures are found early, saving time and compute

explanation: Ordering stages from fastest to slowest gives quick feedback and avoids wasting resources on a broken build.

stem: A front-end build output is stored as a versioned artifact. Why?

options.text: So the same tested build can be deployed to each environment
Because browsers refuse to run unversioned JavaScript files at all
So the source code can be deleted after building
To avoid running any tests on the artifact

explanation: A stored, versioned artifact makes deployments reproducible and rollbacks a matter of redeploying a version.

stem: A pull request from a fork runs your pipeline with secrets exposed. Why is this risky?

options.text: Forks always slow the pipeline down to a crawl
Untrusted code could print or send the secrets to an attacker
Secrets expire as soon as a fork reads them
Pull requests cannot be merged when secrets exist

explanation: A fork's code runs inside your pipeline. Restrict secrets to trusted branches or require approval first.

stem: What does a blue-green deployment need that a simple in-place deployment does not?

options.text: A separate Git repository for each environment
Manual approval for each individual commit
Two production environments so traffic can be switched between them
A rewrite of the application as microservices

explanation: Blue-green runs the new version beside the old one and flips traffic, which gives zero downtime and fast rollback.

stem: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?

options.text: Overloading a server with requests until it stops
Injecting malicious scripts that then run in other users' browsers
Guessing passwords with a list of common words
Intercepting traffic on an unencrypted network

explanation: XSS happens when untrusted input is rendered as code, letting an attacker act as the victim on your site.

stem: What does browser caching save?

options.text: The time the server spends writing its access logs to disk
The effort of compiling the source code
Repeat downloads of files that have not changed
The memory used by the database server

explanation: Cached files are reused from disk, which cuts load time and bandwidth.

stem: Which defence stops another site from submitting forms as a logged-in user (CSRF)?

options.text: Hashing the passwords with a stronger algorithm
Compressing response bodies with gzip
Moving the site to a faster hosting plan
Anti-CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies

explanation: A token the attacker cannot read, or a cookie the browser will not send cross-site, breaks the forged request.

stem: What does code splitting do?

options.text: Loads parts of the app on demand instead of one large bundle
Divides the source code between several developers
Splits every file into one function per file
Stores the bundle on several different servers

explanation: Splitting by route or feature means users download only the code they need first.

stem: Static assets have hashed file names such as app.3f9a.js. Which Cache-Control setting is best?

options.text: no-store so the browser never keeps a copy
A long max-age with immutable, since a change creates a new file name
A max-age of a few seconds so updates appear quickly
no-cache together with a nightly purge of the CDN

explanation: A content hash changes whenever the file does, so old URLs can be cached for a year without going stale.

stem: Which is the most reliable way to stop XSS when rendering user text?

options.text: Strip the word script from every input string
Reject any input that contains a less-than sign
Escape output for its context and set a Content-Security-Policy
Store the input in a database before rendering it

explanation: Blocklists miss variants. Context-aware escaping and a CSP defend regardless of what the input looks like.

stem: What does a load balancer do?

options.text: Stores a copy of every database record
Spreads incoming requests across several servers
Compiles the source code before each new deployment starts
Encrypts the data stored on the disk

explanation: A load balancer shares traffic so no single server is overwhelmed and one failure does not stop the service.

stem: Why put a cache in front of a database?

options.text: To make every write instantly permanent
To replace the need for any database
To serve repeated reads faster and reduce database load
To keep the data private from administrators

explanation: Reads of popular data come from fast memory, so the database handles fewer queries.

stem: A health check fails for one server behind a load balancer. What should happen?

options.text: The balancer restarts the whole fleet of servers
All of the traffic is sent to the failed server to test it out
The balancer deletes the server from the account
The balancer stops sending it traffic until it passes again

explanation: Health checks let the balancer route around a failing instance, which keeps users unaffected.

stem: What is a read replica used for?

options.text: Serving read queries so the primary handles fewer reads
Accepting all of the writes whenever the primary is too busy
Storing the encryption keys for the primary
Compressing the primary's transaction log files

explanation: Replicas copy the primary's data and answer reads. Writes still go to the primary.

stem: What is the core difficulty of cache invalidation?

options.text: Caches cannot store anything bigger than one megabyte
Knowing when cached data is stale without losing the speed benefit
Caches always return data in the wrong order
Invalidation is blocked by most operating systems

explanation: Evict too late and users see old data. Evict too often and the cache stops helping.

stem: What is sharding?

options.text: Copying the same data to several read-only servers
Compressing old rows to save disk space on one server
Splitting data across several databases by a key such as user id
Running two databases as a primary and a standby pair

explanation: Sharding spreads both data and writes, at the cost of harder queries that span shards.
